name: Mandarin
lede: Mandarin is a vivid reddish orange named for the mandarin fruit, a word that also names Chinese officials, a garnet and a style of robe, and the books do not agree on which exact orange it is.

sections.title: Yellow, red-yellow or true orange
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary lists Mandarin as a strong yellow and Mandarin orange, also called Mandarin red, as a reddish yellow [1]. St Clair's glossary instead calls Mandarin a true orange, after the fruit [2]. Books disagree, then, and the swatch here sits at the red end, nearer a vivid [[orange]] than any yellow.

St Clair uses the word for the shade that stands for the Dutch royal house today: she says the orange of the House of Orange was once almost a burnt amber in paintings, and the one favoured now is a sunny mandarin [3].

sections.title: The officials and their squares
sections.body:
The word also means a Chinese official, and the books use it in several unrelated places [4][5][6]. Finlay explains that the Qing inherited the Ming practice of ranking officials with an embroidered silk badge, the mandarin square, showing a bird for a civil servant and an animal for a soldier [4]. In the same trade world, Finlay says Burmese sapphires became blue buttons for mandarin officials and rubies went to imperial headdresses [5]. Paterson notes that crocin, the red powder of Chinese yellow pods, dyed the vestments of mandarins [6].

None of these is the orange of the fruit; they share the word and little else.

sections.title: A garnet called mandarin
sections.body: Finlay lists mandarin among the red garnets: an orange variety from Namibia and Pakistan, alongside brownish almandine, cherry-red pyrope, red-orange spessartine and pinkish rhodolite [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch #F37A48 falls within a color distance of 6 of only 11 paintings in our archive of 23,781, as photographed [8]. It covers at most 45 percent of an Indian court painting from about 1710, and the earliest match is a work attributed to Dürer of 1526 [8]. Orange this saturated is uncommon in these photographs of aged, varnished paintings.
